newsitem.title: UK: BOE's Davies sees new uncertainty over EMU.
newsitem.headline: BOE's Davies sees new uncertainty over EMU.

text.p: Bank of England Deputy governor Howard Davies said the row in Germany over Bundesbank gold reserves and the left's victory in the French election had introduced new uncertainty about the outlook for EMU.

"It is clear that new elements of uncertainty have entered the scene, making it harder than ever to forecast the outcome next year," he told the Futures and Options Association International Derivates Week conference in London.
He did not comment in detail on either the German gold row -- "the Bundesbank's little local difficulty with Herr Waigel" -- or the French election.

Davies said the Bank's interpretation of movements in the forward foreign exchange markets since last autumn was that "markets have become more persuaded that the euro will begin, but that it will be a broader and possibly weaker euro."

"In the last few months the expected future correlation of the deutschemark/dollar and lira/dollar rates has strengthened, suggesting a stronger market expectation of those currencies being part of the first wave," he said.

"Very recently, a few doubts seem to have emerged about the project itself, though it would seem that, acording to the market, the most likely outcome remains that a euro of some sort would start on time."
The Bank's advice remained that it was prudent for businesses to plan on the assumption that the euro would start on January 1, 1999 as stipulated in the Maastricht Treaty.
Davies said he saw no reason why London should suffer as a financial centre even if Britain did not join EMU's first wave.
"Uncertainty about UK participation in EMU has persisted now for a considerable number of years. Yet at the same time, London has remained the dominant futures and options market in Europe."
He said there had been no sign of anticipatory flows of business out of London and into continental European markets.
"London also has a strong clearing function and we should not forget the advantage of the English language which is increasingly the lingua franca of the European Union," he said.

But he said there was no doubt EMU would change things. On-exchange markets would probably only have one three-month euro interest rate futures contract, although a one-month contract may be introduced.
And in the bond markets, the greater depth of the new euro bond market may support a greater range of futures contracts along the yield curve, as in the United States.
"After EMU, one would expect to see the elimination of exchange rate risk narrowing yield differentials," Davies said.
"With exchange rate risk removed and a single monetary policy in operation, national bond yields will differ principally because of differential default risks and differences in market liquidity."
He said EMU could see greater liquidity and tempt new participants into the capital and derivatives markets.
"My hunch is...that the market for carefully constructed derivatives contracts, properly sold to customers with a genuine need for them, will continue to expand."
He said LIFFE has a dominant position in interest rate futures and is a good position to capitalise on that, having already amended contract specifications from March 1999 onwards.

"Those who sieze those opportunities will be the most innovative, most cost effective and most fast moving. At the moment, on this side of the Atlantic, mosrt of those people are found in London. I see no reason why they should move," Davies said.
-- Richard Murphy, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5109
